finding.claim: deleteAccount discards the result of canDelete, so any authenticated non-admin can delete any account they do not own (IDOR / broken object-level authorization).
finding.source: Attacker-controlled path parameter `id` in DELETE /accounts/{id} (src/AccountService.java:20), with `u` as a low-privilege authenticated user (admin=false). Precondition: attacker is logged in and knows or can enumerate another account's id.
finding.sink: accounts.remove(id) at src/AccountService.java:23, a protected destructive operation.

trace.note: deleteAccount(User u, long id) receives the caller and the target id.
a = accounts.get(id) loads the target account, which may be owned by another user.
canDelete(u, a) is called as a bare statement; its boolean return is discarded, so nothing is enforced.
accounts.remove(id) runs unconditionally and deletes the account.

finding.guards_checked: canDelete (src/AccountService.java:9-11) is correct in isolation (admin OR owner) but is never used as a guard on this path. assertCanDelete (lines 13-17), which throws, is not called here. closeAccount (line 29) does call assertCanDelete, so the guard exists but is missing from the delete path. No controller or middleware is in the repo, so no upstream check can be confirmed.

verdict.guard_found: None effective. canDelete (src/AccountService.java:9-11) returns a bool, but line 22 calls it as a bare statement and discards the result. assertCanDelete (lines 13-17) throws on failure, but deleteAccount never calls it. closeAccount (line 29) does call assertCanDelete, so the check exists elsewhere but not on the delete path. No controller or middleware is in the repo, so an upstream check cannot be ruled out.
verdict.reason: deleteAccount at src/AccountService.java:20-23 loads the target at line 21, discards the boolean from canDelete at line 22, and removes the account at line 23, so any caller passing a User with admin=false can delete accounts they do not own. The trace matches the code exactly; the only open point is that the HTTP route and its authentication live outside this repo, so reachability by an authenticated low-privilege user rests on the route's own comment (line 19) and not on code I could read.

finding.claim: Missing-account handling differs from the not-owned case, creating an account-existence oracle and an unhandled NullPointerException for non-admin callers.
finding.source: Attacker-controlled `id` (src/AccountService.java:20 for delete, :27 for close). Precondition: any authenticated non-admin user.
finding.sink: Observable response behaviour and exception type. The NPE is raised at src/AccountService.java:10 when a.ownerId() is dereferenced on null.

trace.note: accounts.get(id) returns null for a nonexistent id.
canDelete(u, null): for a non-admin, u.admin() is false, so line 10 evaluates a.ownerId() on null and throws NullPointerException.

NPE site. An existing account owned by someone else yields a different outcome (silent success today, SecurityException after the AUTHZ-1 fix), so the two cases are distinguishable by status code or exception type.

finding.guards_checked: No null check on `a` before canDelete (line 22) or assertCanDelete (line 29). No 404 path. For admin callers the null case short-circuits at line 10 and silently succeeds.

verdict.guard_found: none. canDelete (src/AccountService.java:9-11) and assertCanDelete (:13-17) have no null check on `a`. Line 22 discards canDelete's return value, so it guards nothing. Line 29 throws on failure, but it dereferences `a` via canDelete before any throw, so it does not help.
verdict.reason: For a non-admin caller, accounts.get(id) returns null for a missing id (src/AccountService.java:21, :28), and a.ownerId() on line 10 then throws NullPointerException from deleteAccount (:22) or closeAccount (:29). An existing account owned by someone else behaves differently: closeAccount throws SecurityException at :15, and deleteAccount silently succeeds because its result is discarded at :22, so existence is distinguishable. Severity is low, because the oracle is only visible to the attacker if the HTTP layer (not in the repo) exposes exception type or status.
